sentences.text: The name Cretoxyrhina combines 'creto' for the Cretaceous period and 'Oxyrhina,' derived from Ancient Greek words meaning 'sharp' and 'nose'.
Its common name, 'Ginsu shark,' was coined in 1999 to describe its slicing and dicing feeding mechanism.
This predator could grow up to 8 meters long and weigh approximately 5000 kilograms.
Its teeth are triangular with razor-like non-serrated edges, visible necks, and a thick enamel coating.
Charles H. Sternberg discovered the first well-preserved skeleton in 1890 and described it in a 1907 paper.
Charles R. Eastman published an analysis of a skeleton in 1894.
A skeleton sold by Sternberg to LMU Munich was destroyed in 1944 by Allied bombing during World War II.
George F. Sternberg found a second skeleton in 1891, now housed in the University of Kansas Museum of Natural History.
It possessed razor-like teeth up to 8 centimeters long with thick enamel designed for stabbing and slicing.
Hydrodynamic calculations suggest it could reach burst speeds of up to 70 kilometers per hour.
Researchers speculate it hunted by lunging at prey at high speeds using strong eyesight, similar to modern great white sharks.
Anatomical analysis suggests it possessed facial and optical features similar to thresher and crocodile sharks and likely used regional endothermy.
While traditionally placed in the family Cretoxyrhinidae, some researchers have proposed classifying it within the families Alopiidae or Lamnidae.
In 1958, Leonid Glickman proposed the new genus Cretoxyrhina based on the dental design of O. mantelli.
Glickman also identified a second species, C. denticulata, based on earlier teeth.
A 2013 study by Mikael Siverson reinstated the genus and moved P. vraconensis into it.
The fossil range of Cretoxyrhina is the Upper Cretaceous.
The earliest fossils date back to approximately 107 million years ago.
The youngest confirmed fossil of C. mantelli dates to 73.2 million years ago and was found in the Bearpaw Formation of Alberta.
Some researchers suggest it may have survived into the Maastrichtian based on a tooth dated to 70.44 million years old, though this is debated due to the deposit being brackish water.
It preferred subtropical to temperate pelagic waters but may have lived in water as cold as 5 degrees Celsius.
Glickman's 1964 replacement of C. mantelli as the type species with 'Isurus denticulatus' is now rejected as an invalid taxonomic amendment.
Viktor Zhelezko erroneously invalidated the genus Cretoxyrhina in 2000 by synonymizing it with 'Pseudoisurus tomosus'.
It is debated whether competition with the giant mosasaur Tylosaurus contributed to the extinction of Cretoxyrhina.
